Demand for Gas in Punjab 
*381. SHRI LAJPAT RAI : Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether there is any proposal for setting up a Core Study Group for 
estimation of demand for Natural Gas/Regassified LNG in Punjab; 
(b) if so, by when the Group would submit its report to Government; 
(c) whether there is any proposal with Government to supply Natural Gas to 
the industrial units in Punjab at the same price at which it is being supplied to 
othef units outside Punjab; and 
(d) if so, the time frame for the implementation of scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM NAIK) 
: (a) No, Sir. However, with reference to such a proposal received from the Punjab 
State Industrial Development Corporation (PSIDC), the Ministry of Petroleum and 
Natural Gas had advised the PSIDC to engage a professional consultancy/agency in 
this regard; PSIDC has since decided to entrust the task to M/s Tata Energy 
Research Institute (TERI). 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) No, sir. 
(d) Does not arise.

Supply of Oil Products from Rajkot Depot 
*382. SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA : Will the MINISTER of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether any representation has been made to restore the supplies of 
oil products from Rajkot depot by Saurashtra-Kutch Petrol and Diesel Dealers' 
Association; 
(b) if so, when; 
(c) whether a joint meeting under his Chairmanship was held on 10th 
March, 2000, in the presence of Minister of State for Heavy Industries and 
Public Enterprises representatives of dealers and officials. 
(d) if so, what was the decision taken; 
(e) whether it is a fact that Minister of State for Heavy Industries and 
Public Enterprises fixed 25th March, 2000, for an on the spot study of the 
problem and visit of the site; and 
(f) if so, the outcome of the study visit ? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (f) A statement is laid on the table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) and (b) Saurashtra -Kutch Petrol -Diesel Dealers' Association 
submitted representations to the Minister of Petroleum & Natural Gas o n 17-
12-1999 and 22- 12-1999 to restore supplies of petroleum products from 
Rajkot Depot. 
(c) to (e) A delegation of Saurashtra -Kutch Petrol -Diesel Dealers' 
Association called on Minister of Petroleum & Natural Gas on 10 -3-2000 
when Minister of State for He avy Industries and Public Enterprises, officials 
of the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas and Oil Companies were also 
present. It was decided that a group comprising the representatives of Dealers' 
Association and Oil Industry would visit Rajkot to exami ne the problems. 
The visit of the delegation was made on 15-4-2000. 
(f) It has now been decided that the supplies of the petroleum products 
from Rajkot Depot would commence shortly.

(a) and (b) After the increase in sale price of DMS milk, the average daily 
sale has declined from around 4.00 lakh litres to 2.36 lakh litres. The reduction is 
41%. 
(c) the following measures have been taken to enhance the sale of DMS milk 
:— 
(1) Commission to the concessionaires & depot agents has been increased; 
(2) Incentive has been introduced to any group of consumers purchasing 
more than 100 litres of milk per day; 
(3) Procedure for issue of home delivery cards has been simplified; 
(4) Depot opening and closing times both for morning and evening shifts 
have been extended; 
(5) New distribution channel of bulk supply has been started; 
(6) Area for supply of DMS milk has been expanded;

oi PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state :

NAIK) :(a) The High Court of Calcutta passed orders on 5th August, 1999 
slaying the operation of the Award No. 1 of 1994 of Central Government 
industrial Tribunal, Calcutta. The award has, therefore, not been implemented. 
(b) Eight out of the total of ten workers involved in the case belong to 
She Scheduled Castes. 
(c) Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas has not issued any directive 
lit ONGC for implementation of the said award. 
(d) No other Tribunal has given any award with regard to sweeping -
cleaning cases concerning ONGC.

whether the ONGC management has filed a case before the Cal cutta High 
Court against Award No. I of 1994 and violated Office Memorandum No. H -
52027/8/99-IR dated the 19 -3-1999 of the Ministry of Labour, Government

Court. The High Court has given a stay to the order of  the Tribunal. In a way,

SHRI KARNENDU BH ATTACH ARJEE : Sir, a number of contractual 
workers were engaged in sweepmg and cleaning jobs in the ONGC offices 
such as Exploration Business Group Office, Regional Office and other offices 
in West Bengal and the North -Eastern Region. 1 would like to know whether

SHRI RAM NAIK : Sir, the facts of the case are that the ONGC had 
given a contract t o a firm M/s. Mondal Enterprises. Now, they engaged nine 
workers to clean the ONGC Offices and that was given on a contract basis. 
Under the Notification of 1976, this type of work is prohibited. But, 
subsequently, the ONGC and some other public sector undertakings were given 
permission to do and get such things done by engaging a firm. So, technically, 
the ONGC —a public sector undertaking —has thought that it is a contractual 
obligation and when that contractual obligation was placed before the Tribuial,

the High Court of Calcutta. There was a preliminary hearing. The High Court 
of Calcutta heard both the sides and then the High Court has given a stay. I 
must also say, as an addi tional information, that there are several such cases 
going on in different High Courts and now the Supreme Court is seized of the 
matter of contractual labour. The Supreme Court also, when the cases were 
referred to them, have broadened the term 'fiill -fledged wage.' The Supreme

concerned, the High Court of Calcutta heard both the sides and given a stay.

*392. SHRI VR DURAISAMY : 
SHRI C.P THIRUNAVUKXARASU :

(b) whether USA's perception of the cross  border terrorism and India's 
compulsions in not signing the CTBT were discussed with him; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) whether Government would institutionalise high-level dialogues and 
economic opportunities between the two countries? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. President Clinton's visit marks a significant and an 
important step in the process of establishing a broad- based and forward 
looking relationship between the two countries. In a Joint Statement signed 
on 21st March, Prime Minister and President Clinton outlined their vision of 
the relationship between India and the United States. They expressed the 
resolve of the two countries to create a closer and qualitatively new 
relationship, based on equality, mutual respect and benefit. 
(b) and (c) The two side discussed all subjects of mutual concern,  
including bilateral, regional and international issues. There is now a better  
appreciation by the United States of the source and nature of cross -border 
terrorism in India. The two sides expressed their determination to intensify  
co-operation   in   combating   terrorism.   Government   also   explained  the  
principles of India's nuclear policy and the reasons that compel India to  
maintain a credible minimum nuclear deterrent. The two sides assessed  
positively their ongoing dialogue on security and non- proliferation and  
agreed to continue the dialogue for further increasing mutual understanding  
and narrowing differences on these issues. President Clinton 
acknowledgedthat India's decision with regard to CTBT would be based on 
the outcome of the democratic process in the country. 
(d) As part of the vision of the new relationship outlined by Prime  
Minister and President Clinton, the two sides have agreed on an architecture 
of a regular, wide- ranging institutional dialogue between the two countries. 
Prime Minister and the US President will hold regular bilateral 'summits'. 
There will also be regular dialogues on foreign policy and security matters at 
the ministerial and ofilc ial levels. A strong institutional framework has also 
been created for dialogue on economic and commercial issues, counter -
terrorism, energy and environment, science and technology.

have been prescribed in the ESI Act, Rules and Regulations framed threunder. 
The workers of closed factories/establishmen ts or those under lock out are

limit of Rs. 20,000 per family per year was used as one of the exclusion criteria 
in the identification of families living below the poverty line under the below 
poverty line (BPL) census conducted by the State Governments at the beginning 
of the Ninth Five Year plan. This exercise is carried out at the beginning of the 
Five Year Plan and not every year, and the income criterion is revised prior to 
each exercise to take into account price increase. 
(b) The Planning Commission estimates the percentage of persons living 
below the poverty line at nat ional and state level on the basis of the 
recommendations of the Expert Group on Estimation of Proportion and Number 
of Poor (Lakdawala Committee). According to this method, the proportion of 
poor in the states are estimated .from the state -specific poverty lines and the 
consumption distribution obtained from the large sample sur \'ey data of the 
National Sample Survey on consumer expenditure conducted by the National 
Sample Surxey Organization (NSSO) at an interval of approximately five years. 
The state-specific poverty lines are estimated by disaggregating the national 
level poverty lines, which are expressed as monthly per capita consumption 
expenditure of Rs. 49.09 in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 in urban areas at 1973 -
74 prices corresponding to a basket of goods and services anchored on a norm 
of per capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 
kcal in urban areas. The disaggregation of the national poverty lines into state 
specific poverty lines is done using state specific price in dices and inter state 
price differential. The number of poor is estimated from the proportion of poor 
and the projected population of the state. This methodology is also adopted for 
West Bengal. The latest estimates of poverty line and poverty in West Bengal 
available for the year 1993-94 are given below :

DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA (West Bengal): Sir, over the last few 
days, we have been discussing many important issues like price rise, the 
brutal attack on the students of Jamia Milia, and the match -fixing issue. But 
during this period, something else was happening, across the seven seas, in 
the West. A storm was brewing. And the eye of the storm was the share 
market in New York. Now, we have not yet experienced the fiiU blast of it. 
It is, probably, yet to come. I hope it does not come. Already, you can see the 
evidence of its impact in different cities; in the different capitals of Asia, and 
within India also. I feel this is something which has to be taken into account 
both by the Government and also by the Parliament, at large.

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2000] 
[THE VICE CHAIRMAN ( SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR) in the 
Chair] Last Friday, the share market prices in the Wail Street in New York fell 
by 9 per cent. Then the Dow Jones Index, which is the relevant index fo r 
assessing the level of activity of the industries, also fell by 6 per cent. That 
was the position last Friday. From this Monday, the Asian markets have come 
under attack. In Japan, the Nikkei benchmark average has come down by 
6.98 per cent. In Australia , it has come down by 5 per cent, including the 
great big empire of Malta. In Hong Kong, it has come down by 8 per cent. In 
Singapore it was reduced by 9 per cent and in Taiwan by 5.4 per cent. 
Obviously, such a big attack on the prices cannot but have som e implications 
on the Indian share market. So, the sensex fell, at least, by 5 per cent or 6 
percent during this period. But much of the fall has been in the prices of 
much-hyped information technology industry. The price of Infosys, of which 
a lot has been said~I hope it is a good company— went down by 18 per cent in 
one day. The current price of Infosys in the Nasdaq share market is less than 
half of what it was on 8th March. The price of Satyam, another much -hyped 
information technology company, is now 20 per cent less of what it was on 
24th February. Wipro is another information technology' company which has 
suffered very badly. We also know that the Zee company and other big global 
companies, which are concerned with media, are also experiencing a big lo ss. 
We also know that early this month there was a crisis in the Indian share 
market because the Indian Government took some action against those 
businessmen who are fraudulently operating from Mauritius and using 
Mauritius as a tax haven. As soon as the G overnment took action against 
them, the prices tumbled and the Government had to eat the humble -pie. It 
withdrew the circular and allowed the fraudulent businessmen to continue 
using Mauritius as a tax haven as before. What is going to happen now? I feel 
there are three things which are very important for us to look at. One is this 
information technology industry, which is talked about as the sun- rise 
industry, an industry which is going to take India to the future, to the 21 st 
century, a industry which is  really achieving the stipulated growth and 
progress for India. Now, unfortunately, this hi -tech industry is also a very 
vulnerable industry, as you can see. If you have followed the prices for the 
last one month, the prices of information technology compa nies continued to 
increase, almost galloped, from what it was in the early Nineties when there 
was a stock -market crash here. There was the securities scam. At that time,  
the prices of these companies, Infosys, Satyam, Wipro-these are the 
174 

[20 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
companies-started galloping. Now we are in a position to know why the 
stock prices are tumbling or falling. It is relted to the speculative action. One 
of the reasons is that we want the information technology to be the key 
industry for India. We have not been realistic. I think we have not floated an 
Indian brand name now. We have been sub -contracting. We are sub-
contracting for the multinational companies. We have no independent 
technology. They tell us what to produce. They give the spec ifications. On 
that basis we produce something. One has to look into the hype about 
information technology industries, the galloping share prices, very clearly. I 
want to ask the Ministry concerned to prepare a report, how many of these 
companies are sub-contracting, to which firm are they sub -contracting and at 
what price? What amount has been paid to our people? So far, no study has 
been made on the information technology industry, although we talk a lot 
about the information technology. 
The second point which I want to make is that we are laying too 
much empahsis on share-marketing since the Nineties. What is the idea? The 
idea is this. The share -market is a part of the globalisation process. It will 
lead to high savings. Now we find that the savings have  gone down. Today, 
the savings are less than what they were in 1991. All that has happened is 
this. The savings, which should have legitimately gone to the banks, have 
been diverted to the share- markets. In fact, they should have been given to 
the insurance companies or banks. We cannot have high savings without high 
income. This is the experience all over the world. There is a great correlation 
between income and savings. In the East Asian countrties, in the initial stage 
the savings were low. But with the  increase in income, the savings went up. 
Now, it has reached a staggering figure of 50 per cent for Singapore and 40 
per cent for other East -Asian countries. Ours is 22 per cent. Savings cannot 
be increased without increasing the income, without increasin g the all -round 
welfare of the country. They should realise that. What is happening is this. 
Because of the hype of the share- market the savings which should have gone 
to the banks and the insurance companies are taken away by it. Even if you 
look at the experience of the East -Asian countries, you will find that the East 
Asian countries have developed, with a high rate of growth of 8% - they did 
not rely on the share market. They relied entirely on banks, on public sector 
banks. This is the basis, this is t he backdrop against which their economy 
prospered and progressed during this period of growth. Now they are in a 
problem. Why? Because, they are also 
175 

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2000] 
speaking of globalisation, going to share markets, etc. And all these pr oblems 
are arising largely because of the way in which they are running their banks. 
Earlier, they were not running them in that way. They are nowgiving too 
much emphasis on the share market. So they are slightly in trouble now. You 
should learn this lesso n from East Asia that banks are the basis of 
development. You should not divert your attention to the share market, where 
there is high speculation. And after some time, you will find it is going up 
some day and going down some day. Not only that; it is re ally making our 
small investors very, very vulnerable. Sir, my third point is this. You must be 
very cautious about globalisation. And if it means globalisation of the people, 
it is okay. But it is globalisation of capital alone and not globalisation of th e 
people. If we want to send the people to Canada or Australia, would they 
accept them? Their immigration control has become stricter. And there is a 
demand on us that you relax import control as far as the capital is concerned. 
We must be very careful because globalisation means we are vulnerable to 
speculation, by what one of the Ministers in England once said, the gnomes of 
Zurich. Earlier, we were exposed to speculation by the hawala people. 
Hawala is bad. But hawala is of a small size compared with the giant 
international corporations which are now speculating in the Indian market. 
And we don't have the resources to fight with these giant international 
corporations who buy and sell in a crisis. Lastly, Sir, sometimes we are told - I 
am saying why I am s o scared about speculation - we have foreign exchange 
reserves of 32 billion dollars. It looks very good. But it is very unreliable. 
Because these foreign exchange reserves have not been built up on the basis of 
export surplus. Wherever the export surplus is the basis of foreign exchange 
reserves, then it is solid. Our foreign exchange reserves have been built up by 
borro^ving and also by speculating on money, which has been controlled in 
the past. It can disappear any moment. In ten days these 32 billion d ollars 
could melt away, through speculation. That is the experience of England; that 
is the experience of the East Asian countries. We are in for a very dangerous 
situation. I request all of you to look into this. I hope nothing much happen. 
But even today, I find that the value of rupee is going down. Today, the value 
of rupee has reached its lowest level over the last 21 months. For the last 
almost two years, it will be the lowest value of the rupee. Speculation against 
the rupee has started. I hope the G overnment is keeping a watch on the 
developments. I am saying this because it is a very ominous development. I 
do not want to cause panic.

[20 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
But we must be concerned and informed. I am sure the Government will keep

how their shares are gallopping and tumbling and also the unnecessary betting

Entry of Bangladeshi citizens into the voters list of Assam 
DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA (Assam): Mr. Vice- Chairman, Sir, 
through you, I would like to draw the attention of this House and also of the 
Government to a very sensitive issue pertaining to the entire country and 
specifically to the State of Assam. Sir, the unfortunate cons equences of 
partition led to a large -scale infiltration from Pakistan and later from 
Bangladesh into various States of the country. The situation in Assam in this 
regard is very alarming.    The State of Assam had to take the burden of a 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2000] 
large number of refugees who had come from different parts of East Pakistan 
of that time. There was Nehru -Liyaqat Ali Pact 1950 and then there was 
Indira-Mujib Pact 1971. Through these Pacts there were a lot of national 
commitments and a la rge chunk of foreign population had to be accepted in 
Assam. Some of them were given citizenship certificates in terms of the 
Assam Accord also. There was a six -year long agitation on this particular 
issue because this population which had been accepted in a large number is a 
threat to the political identity of the Indian population who are living there 
since before partition. The situation has become more alarming very recently 
and there is a report of the Home Ministry in this regard. I want to cite it. I t 
appeared in The Sentinel, which is published from Guwahati, on March 2, 
2000.The heading is: "Illegal migrants constitute majority in 36 
constituencies." The Report says, "The Home Ministry is extremely 
concerned that illegal migrants from Banglandesh co nstitute the majority of 
the voters in as many as 36 Assembly Constituencies of Assam, out of the 
total of 126 Constituencies, and have acquired the vantage position to 
determine the political lives of all sections of the indigenous people. The 
Ministry has already drawn up the list of these 36 Constituencies and sent it to 
the State Government and all other agencies concerned under it to draw their 
attention to this highly worrisome fact and devise appropriate measures in 
close consultation with each other ." This is a very sensitive issue. Very 
gradually, with a silent invasion, the political rights of our indigenous citizens 
have been taken over step -by-step. If adequate steps are not taken, probably, 
50 per cent of the constituencies in Assam would be inf luenced by the voters 
who have crossed over to Assam from Bangladesh, at various points of time. 
There is a history that we must know as to how these voters got the advantage 
of their names being entered in the voters' list. Sir, the Election Commission 
has a procedure. First, the Election Commission enumerates the population 
before the preparation of the voters' list. When the voters' list is under 
preparation, a draft roll would be published. After that, on the basis of the 
draft roll, if there is no obje ction from the local citizens, the draft roll would 
be published as the final list. Now, it is very difficult to enumerate or find out 
as to who is a Bangladeshi citizen or who is an Indian citizen. So, all the 
names are collected and they are scrutinised by the Electoral Registration 
Officer. What was the major defect? The major defect is, every Electoral 
Registration Officer has to scrutinise more than 15,000 to 20,000 people at a 
time. As per the election law, he will be given fifteen days' time to scrutinise 
186 

[20 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the citizenship status of 15,000 -20,000 doubtful citizens. Suppose, if some 
citizens file an objection, he has to scrutinise that. He has also to scrutinise 
the status of those people who claim that they are also the citizens of the 
country. And, he will be given only 15 days'time. It is humanly impossible to 
hear everybody, to summon documents from everybody, and the situation is 
very grim because each and every Bangladeshi citizen living in Assam is 
now having a fal se citizenship certificate. They print false voters' list as 
reference. They used to claim, "My father's name is there in the 1966 voters' 
list." The 1966 original voters' list of a particular constituency is not being 
circulated to all over the constituen cies of Assam. So, when he claims, it is 
very difficult for the Electoral Registration Officer to ascertain whether a 
particular person's father had been living in other constituencies of the State 
in 1966. And, the Election Commission is also not maintain ing these original 
documents properly. That is the reason why, gradually, the political destiny 
of Assam has been going into the hands of the people to whom we have given 
shelter and to whom we have shown sympathy. The question is, the 
Government of India have two different views towards Bangladesh and 
Pakistan. Sir, Bangladesh is always treated as a friendly country, and we 
have some liberal view on it, towards Pakistan, it is the other way round. 
Through the Indo -Bangladesh border, a large -scale migration  is still taking 
place, and, every year, and during every election, their names are entered in 
the voters' list. So, Sir, my humble request to the Government, and also to the 
Election Commission is, please find out a special mechanism for Assam, if 
we want to save this area from the hands of these silent invaders. Some ISI 
activists were arrested last year, in the month of July, in Assam, where a 
blueprint was detected. It was said that the ISI had a design to annex Assam, 
and also some parts of the other N orth-Eastern States, with Bangladesh in 
near fiiture. They are coming very silently. It is the responsibility of the 
entire country not to leave this issue, as merely an issue of the Assamese 
community, as an issue of Assam Gana Parishad, or of All Assam S tudents' 
Union, which carried on an agitation of six long years in accordance with 
Gandhian principles. 1 hope, the Government and the Election Commission 
will evolve another special scrutiny procedure for Assam so that the false 
citizenship certificate and the false voters list which have so far been used by 
the illegal migrants, are not used any more, and they are properly detected, 
and the Electoral Registration Officer is given sufficient time so that he can 
apply his mind; he   can identify and verify each and every document. He can 
187 

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2000] 
perform his functions judiciously to verify the citizenship status of every 
citizen in Assam. If the normal procedure is followed, this problem can never 
be solved. Therefore, I request that  special attention may be given on this 
particular issue. Thank you. Sir.

the problems which Dr. Sarma has enumerated in such a detail, more or less, 
pertains to all the States in that area; but restricting myself to Assam, in  
addition to the problem which Dr. Sarma has identified, Assam, now, has 
become a thoroughfare for illegal immigrants passing through Assam, going 
to Bhutan and other places of India also. Iminigrants are of three types. They

ago, had said that this was a problem for which they would have to find a 
solution. Some kind of issue of temporary work permit, etc. But that is with

districts of Assam, wiiich are most affected, as my hon. friend has mentioned,

Army, South Assam, Kachar, Haplong, Karbianglong. A sftuation has come

demographic border of India and Bangladesh are different. The political 
border is where it is, the geographic border. The demographic border extends

border in not being treated with the same degree of concern as in the case of 
the western border. It has been our experience that the western border;

immigrants who have come from across the border, who have settled down,

to the eastern border, as it is giving to the western border. Thank you, Mr.

situation the country is facing is a very dangerous one. They have to make it 
clear as to what the objectives are and how they are going to achieve them, 
whether the existing provisions of the Constitution are not capable of 
achieving those objectives and whether the entire review is warranted. 
Sir, to what extent the proposed review of the Constitution is going 
to improve the standard of living of the people? Moreover, no terms of 
reference have been made. Unfortunately, the polity in India is being 
disrespected and it has not been taken into confidence. The best judges of the 
performance of the Constitution are the elected representatives, the people's 
representatives; they have been totally ignored. They s hould have been taken 
into confidence to fix the terms of reference. It is not somebody sitting in the

confidence in us and we are the best judges. I should say that the Government

Government should come out with its motivations clearly. Sir, the BJP has

Government has not done so. The Government should have come out with a

good intentions but your intentions should be made clear to the people. They 
should not create any misapprehension among the people which has already 
been created. It is our duty to clear it. Otherwise, it is a very dangerous thing 
which is going to come. Sir, I am constrained to say, whether it is rational or 
irrational, I cannot judge - that the proposed review is aimed at and detrimental 
to the intere sts of the Dalits of this country. And what I am telling you is

Government. You should have those bonafides; you should have those 
credentials to allay the misapprehensions. Otherwise,  why should crores and 
crores of people have such apprehensions in their minds? At least, if you feel 
at all that it is propaganda, you should come out with your propaganda 
machinery to allay those fears. Sir, there are certain areas where the 
Constitution is required to be amended because various political parties have 
got their own perceptions with regard to the appointment of judges. The 
elected Parliament or the Government does not have the power to appoint the 
judges. It is now left to the discretion o f the judiciary. Most of the parties 
want that those powers should be restored back to the Parliament or the 
Government. So, this is where the Constitution needs to be amended. Sir, the 
issue of reservation for th SCs and STs and to the total disliking of the other 
side, the issue where there are some parties who subscribe to the concept that 
the people who have not taken birth in this country should be elevated to the 
important positions, are also areas where the Constitution needs to be 
amended. The Centr e-State relations, devolution of powers, financial and 
executive, bringing about a more federal structure, are the areas
